Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Learning Objectives
Write Structured Scenarios
Use the six-part template to make responses measurable and testable. Each field answers a clear question: who triggers it, what happens, which component is involved, where it occurs, how the system should react, and how success is measured.
Mnemonic

screens.title: What Is a Quality Attribute?
screens.narratorSegment: A quality attribute is a non-functional characteristic that describes how well a system performs rather than what it does. Where a functional requirement names a capability, like "process a payment," a quality attribute describes performance, security, availability, scalability, maintainability, usability, or deployability — attributes that shape design choices. For instance, an e-commerce site may prioritize availability and performance during peak sales, while a medical device system may prioritize reliability and safety even at the cost of some performance. That contrast matters because the chosen attribute priorities drive component selection, redundancy decisions, and testing strategies. A common misconception is to treat quality attributes as vague goals; instead, they must be expressed in measurable terms to guide architecture. Example: performance as a requirement becomes "95% of dashboard views render within 200 milliseconds under normal load." In practice, clear attributes let you compare architectures by asking: which design best satisfies the prioritized attributes and at what cost? Takeaway: always translate attributes into measurable expectations before design or evaluation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Quality Attribute Workshop (QAW) Overview
screens.narratorSegment: A Quality Attribute Workshop is a facilitated, structured meeting where architects, developers, product owners, and operators collaborate to identify and prioritize the system's most important quality attributes and their scenarios. The workshop begins with an introduction to attributes and why they matter. Then stakeholders brainstorm candidate attributes and propose scenarios. The facilitator guides the discussion to ensure scenarios are specific, measurable, and include context. Avoid free-form lists of abstract attributes; instead insist on scenario detail. During the workshop participants also prioritize scenarios by impact and likelihood so limited design effort is focused. A common mistake is to let a vocal attendee dominate or to accept vague statements without measurable response measures. The outcome of a QAW is a set of prioritized, structured scenarios that feed into architecture evaluation, risk analysis, and design trade-offs. Example: a QAW for a payment system surfaces a prioritized list emphasizing transactional security, peak performance during sales, and a recovery time objective for outages. The workshop makes implicit expectations explicit, which saves costly revisions later. Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › QAW Overview
Workshop flow
Step 1
Introduce quality attributes and the goal of the workshop.
Step 2
Brainstorm attribute candidates and propose scenario ideas with context.
Step 3
Refine scenarios to include measures and environmental conditions.
Step 4
Prioritize scenarios by impact and likelihood.
Key facilitation tips
  • Encourage concrete examples, not abstract labels. Ask "how will we measure success?"
  • Include diverse stakeholders so operational and business perspectives appear.
  • Prevent vague acceptance: require environment and response measures for each scenario.
  • Use prioritization to focus subsequent design and evaluation work.
Outcome
A prioritized, measurable scenario set that architects can use to probe design.
Common mistake
Accepting generic attributes without scenario context, which leaves design choices unconstrained.

screens.title: Eliciting Scenarios: Types and Intent
screens.narratorSegment: Scenarios are short, concrete stories that make a quality attribute actionable. There are three useful types. Operational scenarios, or use cases, describe expected behavior under normal conditions — for example, a user logs in and sees their dashboard within two seconds. Growth scenarios describe how the system must adapt over time, such as supporting a specified increase in concurrent users or adding features with minimal redesign. Exploratory scenarios, also called stress or failure cases, show how the system should behave under extreme or unusual conditions, like component failure or attack. Each type serves a different purpose in evaluation: operational scenarios validate everyday correctness and performance; growth scenarios reveal how design supports evolution; exploratory scenarios uncover resilience and limits. A frequent misconception is to treat exploratory cases as less important; in reality they reveal key architectural weaknesses. When eliciting scenarios in a QAW, target all three types so the architecture is validated for normal operation, evolution, and stress. This balanced coverage gives a comprehensive picture of risks and design needs. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Eliciting Scenarios
Operational (Use Case)
Describes normal system behavior under typical conditions. Example: a user logs in and sees their dashboard within two seconds.
Purpose
Validate everyday performance and correctness.
Growth (Evolutionary)
Describes how the system must adapt to predictable changes. Example: support a 50% increase in concurrent users within six months without major redesign.
Purpose
Assess architecture readiness for expansion and change.
Exploratory (Stress)
Describes behavior under extreme or failure conditions. Example: automatic failover within 30 seconds after a primary database failure.
Purpose
Reveal resilience, failure modes, and recovery expectations.
Facilitation note
Ensure the QAW solicits at least one scenario of each type. Skipping exploratory cases leaves critical risks undiscovered; skipping growth cases hides long-term costs.

screens.title: Scenario Structure: The Six Fields
screens.narratorSegment: Every useful scenario follows a clear structure so architects can evaluate and test it. The template has six fields: Source, Stimulus, Artifact, Environment, Response, and Response Measure. Source names who or what initiates the event, such as a user, operator, or external attacker. Stimulus is the event that triggers the behavior, for example a surge of requests or a failed node. Artifact is the part of the system affected — a service, database, or network. Environment describes the conditions, like production during peak hours or degraded network. Response explains how the system should react, and Response Measure gives a quantifiable success metric, such as a recovery time or tolerance level. Using this template stops vague statements and ensures each scenario contains testable acceptance criteria. A misconception to avoid is leaving out the environment or a measurable response; such omissions make evaluation subjective. Practice filling each field for a single scenario to confirm clarity and measurability. In practical terms, template that makes a scenario clear and measurable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Scenario Structure
Six fields
  • Source: who or what initiates the action.
  • Stimulus: the triggering event.
  • Artifact: the component or subsystem involved.
  • Environment: conditions under which the stimulus occurs.
  • Response: how the system reacts.
  • Response Measure: quantifiable success criteria.
Example field
Response Measure might be a recovery time objective or a percentage of successful requests, which makes acceptance testable.
Practice card
Fill the six fields for a single scenario. If any field is missing or imprecise, iterate until you have a measurable response measure and clear environment definition.
Common error
Skipping environment or using vague measures like "fast" rather than a numeric target.
Pro tip
Prefer percentages and time bounds (e.g., 99.5% requests under 300 ms) to make testing straightforward.

screens.title: Worked Example: Authentication Service Security Scenario
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete scenario using the six-field template for an authentication service focusing on security. Imagine the Source is an unauthorized external attacker. The Stimulus is the attacker attempting 100 login attempts within 10 seconds using various credentials. The Artifact is the User Authentication Service. The Environment is the production system under normal load. The Response is that the service detects the brute-force pattern and temporarily blocks the attacker's IP for five minutes. The Response Measure is twofold: fewer than one percent of legitimate users are impacted by the block, and the attacker cannot continue attempts during the block window. This example shows how specific and measurable expectations replace the vague requirement "the system must be secure." A common misconception is to think "security" can be satisfied by naming controls; instead, the scenario forces you to assess whether design choices, like rate limiting and logging, actually meet the measurable outcome. Takeaway: structured examples let you validate proposed design elements against a clear acceptance criterion. Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Authentication Scenario
Filled template
Source: Unauthorized external attacker
Stimulus: 100 login attempts within 10 seconds using various credentials
Artifact: User Authentication Service
Environment: Production, normal load
Response: Detect brute-force pattern and temporarily block attacker's IP for 5 minutes
Response Measure: Less than 1% legitimate user impact; attacker prevented for block duration
Design probes
Which design elements satisfy detection and blocking with this response measure? Consider rate limiting, IDS rules, and logging for forensics.
Architecture implications
  • Rate limiting at edge vs service-level limits affects false positive rates and legitimate user impact.
  • Blocking by IP requires consideration of NAT, proxies, and legitimate shared addresses.
  • Logging and monitoring must support detection within the time window.
Key Takeaway

A structured scenario connects concrete requirements to architectural questions and measurable acceptance criteria.

screens.title: Operational vs Growth vs Exploratory — Contrast
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing scenario types clarifies why you need all three during evaluation. Operational scenarios test the system under expected use and reveal performance bottlenecks, user-facing latency, and correctness issues. Growth scenarios test adaptability and evolution, exposing where modularity, extensibility, and scalability matter; they often highlight costs of change and migration paths. Exploratory scenarios stress resilience and failure recovery, making redundancy, failover logic, and graceful degradation requirements explicit. Consider a web store: an operational scenario checks that product pages load quickly; a growth scenario asks whether the architecture supports doubling peak users without a major redesign; an exploratory scenario simulates a database outage and demands automatic failover with no data loss. A common mistake is assuming a design that meets operational targets will automatically meet growth or exploratory needs; it often will not. Use-case alone can hide scaling limits or brittle failure modes. Closing question: which scenario type most often reveals hidden costs in your current systems — operational, growth, or exploratory? The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Prioritizing and Refining Scenarios
screens.narratorSegment: After scenarios are elicited in a QAW, the next step is prioritization and refinement. Prioritization typically considers impact and likelihood: how much a scenario affects business goals and how likely it is to occur. Refinement adds missing context and measurable response measures so each scenario can be evaluated. The goal is a focused set of scenarios that drive architecture effort. For example, a high-impact, high-likelihood scenario such as secure transactions during peak sales should be prioritized over a low-likelihood exploratory case. But beware: deprioritizing exploratory cases entirely can hide catastrophic risks. Use a small matrix or weighted scoring to record rationale. Once prioritized, refine scenarios by tightening the environment, defining response measures, and clarifying any assumptions. This yields scenarios that are both actionable and auditable. Architects then probe the design: what components are sensitive to this scenario, what are the trade-offs, and what mitigations or patterns are available? The prioritized scenarios become the backbone of evaluation and design decisions. In practical terms, turn many candidate scenarios into a focused evaluation set. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Using Scenarios to Probe Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Once you have prioritized, measurable scenarios, use them to probe the architecture. Probing means asking targeted questions: which components participate, what are single points of failure, how do data flows change under the scenario, and what are the performance or security implications? For example, a scenario requiring sub-second responses might force you to cache data closer to users, introduce read replicas, or adopt asynchronous processing — each choice has trade-offs such as increased complexity or weaker consistency. Another example: an exploratory failover scenario may show the need for geographically redundant data stores but also surface increased latency and consistency challenges. Architects should document sensitivities and trade-offs discovered during probes, then propose mitigations and acceptance criteria. A common misconception is to treat probes as one-off checks; instead, they should produce actionable items and measurable expectations for design iterations. Closing question: what architectural element in your system is most sensitive to prioritized scenarios? Activity instructions
  1. Choose two quality attributes critical to a real-time trading platform.

Example (Operational)

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Pro Tips
screens.narratorSegment: When running QAWs and writing scenarios, teams commonly fall into a few traps. First, leaving attributes vague — saying "the system must be fast" without a response measure — makes evaluation impossible. Second, accepting scenarios without an environment hides assumptions about load, failure conditions, or operational configuration. Third, allowing a single stakeholder to dominate can skew priorities toward narrow concerns. To avoid these mistakes, require S-S-A-E-R-M fields for every scenario, insist on numeric response measures, and include operators and business owners in the conversation. Pro tips: frame exploratory scenarios as experiments to reveal limits rather than rare hypotheticals to ignore; use small scoring rubrics to justify prioritization decisions; and treat scenarios as living artifacts that may be refined as you prototype. Example practice: after drafting scenarios, run a short tabletop review to spot missing assumptions and to agree on measurable responses. Closing reflection: which one mistake do you most need to stop doing in your next workshop? fullNarratorScript:
We begin with a practical promise: quality attributes are the criteria by which a design succeeds, and Quality Attribute Workshops are the structured way to find those criteria. In this lesson you will learn what quality attributes are, how a facilitated workshop surfaces concrete scenarios, and why those scenarios are essential for making architecture decisions. Think of a quality attribute as how well a system behaves — for example, how fast it responds, how resilient it is to failures, or how safely it protects data. A workshop gathers stakeholders so those abstract concerns become specific, measurable stories about system behavior. You will see examples of operational, growth, and exploratory scenarios and learn a reliable template to write them clearly. We will also cover common mistakes: vague attributes, missing measures, or leaving out the environment. By the end you'll understand how scenarios inform prioritization, reveal trade-offs, and feed formal evaluations. Keep in mind: the stronger your scenarios, the clearer the architecture review and the fewer hidden risks remain. How will this change the way you describe non-functional needs?

These objectives guide our focus so you will leave able to turn non-functional goals into concrete, testable scenarios. First, you will define and differentiate key quality attributes such as performance, security, availability, scalability, maintainability, and usability, learning the language architects use to compare designs. Second, you will understand the purpose and structure of a Quality Attribute Workshop — why it is facilitated, who participates, and how it produces prioritized inputs for architecture evaluation. Each objective includes a practical mnemonic to help you remember the core idea and a competency milestone to verify understanding. You'll see examples and brief contrasts so you can spot common confusions, like treating quality attributes as features rather than measures. By mastering these skills you will ensure the architecture can be measured and validated against real expectations. This makes requirements actionable and reduces late surprises during implementation.

In the second objectives slide we focus on doing. You will learn to write well-formed scenarios using the template that includes source, stimulus, artifact, environment, response, and response measure. Then you will practice prioritizing scenarios so limited design effort targets the highest risks and most important qualities. Finally, you will use scenarios to probe architecture: translate a scenario into questions about components, dependencies, and failure modes. Each objective is framed by why it matters: measures enable testing, prioritization prevents wasted work, and probing reveals hidden trade-offs. A short mnemonic accompanies each skill to help you retain the steps during a workshop. By treating scenarios as living evaluation artifacts you keep architecture discussions evidence-based rather than opinion-based. This reduces rework and clarifies acceptance criteria for non-functional goals. Learning Objectives — Practice & Application means writing and prioritizing scenarios gives architects concrete inputs to validate design decisions and manage trade-offs.. In practical terms, skills for writing, prioritizing, and using scenarios. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A quality attribute is a non-functional characteristic that describes how well a system performs rather than what it does. Where a functional requirement names a capability, like "process a payment," a quality attribute describes performance, security, availability, scalability, maintainability, usability, or deployability — attributes that shape design choices. For instance, an e-commerce site may prioritize availability and performance during peak sales, while a medical device system may prioritize reliability and safety even at the cost of some performance. That contrast matters because the chosen attribute priorities drive component selection, redundancy decisions, and testing strategies. A common misconception is to treat quality attributes as vague goals; instead, they must be expressed in measurable terms to guide architecture. Example: performance as a requirement becomes "95% of dashboard views render within 200 milliseconds under normal load." In practice, clear attributes let you compare architectures by asking: which design best satisfies the prioritized attributes and at what cost? Takeaway: always translate attributes into measurable expectations before design or evaluation. What Is a Quality Attribute? means quality attributes describe how well a system behaves and must be measurable to guide architecture.. In practical terms, non-functional characteristics that define how well a system performs its functions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Quality Attribute Workshop is a facilitated, structured meeting where architects, developers, product owners, and operators collaborate to identify and prioritize the system's most important quality attributes and their scenarios. The workshop begins with an introduction to attributes and why they matter. Then stakeholders brainstorm candidate attributes and propose scenarios. The facilitator guides the discussion to ensure scenarios are specific, measurable, and include context. Avoid free-form lists of abstract attributes; instead insist on scenario detail. During the workshop participants also prioritize scenarios by impact and likelihood so limited design effort is focused. A common mistake is to let a vocal attendee dominate or to accept vague statements without measurable response measures. The outcome of a QAW is a set of prioritized, structured scenarios that feed into architecture evaluation, risk analysis, and design trade-offs. Example: a QAW for a payment system surfaces a prioritized list emphasizing transactional security, peak performance during sales, and a recovery time objective for outages. The workshop makes implicit expectations explicit, which saves costly revisions later. Quality Attribute Workshop (QAW) Overview means qaws gather stakeholders to turn implicit expectations into prioritized, measurable scenarios for architecture evaluation.. In practical terms, a structured session to surface and prioritize scenarios. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Scenarios are short, concrete stories that make a quality attribute actionable. There are three useful types. Operational scenarios, or use cases, describe expected behavior under normal conditions — for example, a user logs in and sees their dashboard within two seconds. Growth scenarios describe how the system must adapt over time, such as supporting a specified increase in concurrent users or adding features with minimal redesign. Exploratory scenarios, also called stress or failure cases, show how the system should behave under extreme or unusual conditions, like component failure or attack. Each type serves a different purpose in evaluation: operational scenarios validate everyday correctness and performance; growth scenarios reveal how design supports evolution; exploratory scenarios uncover resilience and limits. A frequent misconception is to treat exploratory cases as less important; in reality they reveal key architectural weaknesses. When eliciting scenarios in a QAW, target all three types so the architecture is validated for normal operation, evolution, and stress. This balanced coverage gives a comprehensive picture of risks and design needs. Eliciting Scenarios: Types and Intent means use operational, growth, and exploratory scenarios to exercise normal behavior, evolution, and failure modes.. In practical terms, operational, growth, and exploratory scenarios explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Every useful scenario follows a clear structure so architects can evaluate and test it. The template has six fields: Source, Stimulus, Artifact, Environment, Response, and Response Measure. Source names who or what initiates the event, such as a user, operator, or external attacker. Stimulus is the event that triggers the behavior, for example a surge of requests or a failed node. Artifact is the part of the system affected — a service, database, or network. Environment describes the conditions, like production during peak hours or degraded network. Response explains how the system should react, and Response Measure gives a quantifiable success metric, such as a recovery time or tolerance level. Using this template stops vague statements and ensures each scenario contains testable acceptance criteria. A misconception to avoid is leaving out the environment or a measurable response; such omissions make evaluation subjective. Practice filling each field for a single scenario to confirm clarity and measurability. Let's walk through a concrete scenario using the six-field template for an authentication service focusing on security. Imagine the Source is an unauthorized external attacker. The Stimulus is the attacker attempting 100 login attempts within 10 seconds using various credentials. The Artifact is the User Authentication Service. The Environment is the production system under normal load. The Response is that the service detects the brute-force pattern and temporarily blocks the attacker's IP for five minutes. The Response Measure is twofold: fewer than one percent of legitimate users are impacted by the block, and the attacker cannot continue attempts during the block window. This example shows how specific and measurable expectations replace the vague requirement "the system must be secure." A common misconception is to think "security" can be satisfied by naming controls; instead, the scenario forces you to assess whether design choices, like rate limiting and logging, actually meet the measurable outcome. Comparing scenario types clarifies why you need all three during evaluation. Operational scenarios test the system under expected use and reveal performance bottlenecks, user-facing latency, and correctness issues. Growth scenarios test adaptability and evolution, exposing where modularity, extensibility, and scalability matter; they often highlight costs of change and migration paths. Exploratory scenarios stress resilience and failure recovery, making redundancy, failover logic, and graceful degradation requirements explicit. Consider a web store: an operational scenario checks that product pages load quickly; a growth scenario asks whether the architecture supports doubling peak users without a major redesign; an exploratory scenario simulates a database outage and demands automatic failover with no data loss. A common mistake is assuming a design that meets operational targets will automatically meet growth or exploratory needs; it often will not. Use-case alone can hide scaling limits or brittle failure modes. Closing question: which scenario type most often reveals hidden costs in your current systems — operational, growth, or exploratory? After scenarios are elicited in a QAW, the next step is prioritization and refinement. Prioritization typically considers impact and likelihood: how much a scenario affects business goals and how likely it is to occur. Refinement adds missing context and measurable response measures so each scenario can be evaluated. The goal is a focused set of scenarios that drive architecture effort. For example, a high-impact, high-likelihood scenario such as secure transactions during peak sales should be prioritized over a low-likelihood exploratory case. But beware: deprioritizing exploratory cases entirely can hide catastrophic risks. Use a small matrix or weighted scoring to record rationale. Once prioritized, refine scenarios by tightening the environment, defining response measures, and clarifying any assumptions. This yields scenarios that are both actionable and auditable. Architects then probe the design: what components are sensitive to this scenario, what are the trade-offs, and what mitigations or patterns are available? The prioritized scenarios become the backbone of evaluation and design decisions. Once you have prioritized, measurable scenarios, use them to probe the architecture. Probing means asking targeted questions: which components participate, what are single points of failure, how do data flows change under the scenario, and what are the performance or security implications? For example, a scenario requiring sub-second responses might force you to cache data closer to users, introduce read replicas, or adopt asynchronous processing — each choice has trade-offs such as increased complexity or weaker consistency. Another example: an exploratory failover scenario may show the need for geographically redundant data stores but also surface increased latency and consistency challenges. Architects should document sensitivities and trade-offs discovered during probes, then propose mitigations and acceptance criteria. A common misconception is to treat probes as one-off checks; instead, they should produce actionable items and measurable expectations for design iterations. When running QAWs and writing scenarios, teams commonly fall into a few traps. First, leaving attributes vague — saying "the system must be fast" without a response measure — makes evaluation impossible. Second, accepting scenarios without an environment hides assumptions about load, failure conditions, or operational configuration. Third, allowing a single stakeholder to dominate can skew priorities toward narrow concerns. To avoid these mistakes, require S-S-A-E-R-M fields for every scenario, insist on numeric response measures, and include operators and business owners in the conversation. Pro tips: frame exploratory scenarios as experiments to reveal limits rather than rare hypotheticals to ignore; use small scoring rubrics to justify prioritization decisions; and treat scenarios as living artifacts that may be refined as you prototype. Example practice: after drafting scenarios, run a short tabletop review to spot missing assumptions and to agree on measurable responses. To close, remember three central ideas. First, quality attributes are non-functional characteristics like performance, security, and availability; they must be expressed as measurable expectations to guide architecture. Second, a Quality Attribute Workshop is a facilitated process that converts stakeholder concerns into prioritized, testable scenarios; it prevents vague requirements and surfaces trade-offs early. Third, scenarios follow a six-field template — Source, Stimulus, Artifact, Environment, Response, Response Measure — which makes them actionable and testable. Keeping scenarios measurable and prioritized lets you probe architecture effectively and reveal design sensitivities.
